Abstract
Physical reservoir computing (PRC) offers an effective computing paradigm for
spatiotemporal information processing with low training costs. Achieving con-
trollable regulation over the temporal dynamics of devices to meet the compu-
tational demands of each physical layer is a key challenge for realizing high-
performance PRC chips. Here, we proposed a homogeneously integrated all-
PRC with tunable temporal dynamics. Utilizing the modulation effect of oxy-
gen vacancies on the energy barrier of the pentacene/ZnO interface, short-
term memory, and long-term memory switching characteristics have been
achieved within the same device structure. Furthermore, by altering the gate
voltage, the reservoir exhibited a broad range ratio of temporal characteristics
(>102), which provides the potential to map information with different tempo-
ral characteristics. Inspired by the process of encoding and reconstructing spa-
tiotemporal information in the human visual system, a biomimetic obstacle
recognition system has been constructed to assist visually impaired individuals
in walking, demonstrating excellent accuracy in obstacle types (100%) and dis-
tances (97.2%) recognition. This work offers a promising avenue for the devel-
opment of an integrated PRC system with multi-timescale information
processing capability.

INTRODUCTION
The computing paradigm of the human brain's low-
power, high-efficiency parallel information processing
has inspired the development of neuromorphic comput-
ing architectures to adapt to the era of big data.1–5 Physi-
cal reservoir computing (PRC) leverages real physical
devices as reservoirs, providing significant advantages in
the processing of spatiotemporal information with low
training costs.6–8 The reservoirs require devices with
short-term memory (STM) characteristics to replace com-
plex recursive networks and couple the temporal correla-
tions of input signals.9,10 The output layer performs a
typical vector-matrix multiplication (VMM) operation by
multiplying the state vector with the output weights.11
Therefore, the devices used in the output layer must pos-
sess long-term memory (LTM) characteristics to store the
trained output weights (Figure 1).12 Although a large
number of neuromorphic devices have been applied to
PRC in recent years, the majority of these reservoirs only
have a narrow range ratio of temporal characteristics (τ,
<15).13–16 However, in the open-world, external spatio-
temporal information is typically complex and across
multi-timescale.17 For instance, when performing recog-
nition of external obstacles with different input frequen-
cies, a limited range ratio of τ is not conducive to
expanding the number of effective reservoir node states
and restricts
the
reservoir
size, thereby preventing
the
reservoir
from
extracting
information
across
multi-timescale. This severely limits the accuracy of rec-
ognition. Currently, by modulating the redistribution of
electrons among the oxygen vacancies in the ZnO layer
through gate voltage, PRC with controllable temporal
dynamics can recognize objects moving at a wide range
of speeds in real time.18 Additionally, by coupling multi-
variate physics mechanisms into a single vertical transis-
tor to enrich the dynamics of photogenerated excitons,
grouped-reservoir
computing
has
achieved
traffic
trajectory prediction that includes signals with different
spatiotemporal characteristics.19 While the aforemen-
tioned works have achieved reservoirs with a broad range
ratio of τ, the output layer is implemented purely through
algorithms, without further careful design of device char-
acteristics to meet the LTM requirements of the output
layer.
Additionally, to simplify the algorithm and reduce
computational load, the output layer requires LTM
devices
for
weight
updates.20,21
By
introducing
or
avoiding imprint fields in the ferroelectric layer to con-
struct STM/LTM memristors, all-ferroelectric PRC for
temporary tasks such as curvature discrimination has
been reported.22 Besides, coupling the STM caused by
charge-trapping/detrapping with the LTM induced by fer-
roelectric polarization can enhance the richness of the
reservoir states, thereby providing a reconfigurable PRC
with
expanded
capacity.23
Nevertheless,
the
above-
mentioned PRC construct with devices of different
switching characteristics is limited by a narrow ratio
range of τ (<4), which restricts the reservoir size and the
ability to process information across multi-timescale.
Therefore, for the future development of monolithic
three-dimensional (3D) integration of PRC chips, there is
an urgent need to develop physical devices with tunable
temporal dynamics, that is, a broad range ratio of τ and
reconfigurable STM/LTM characteristics, to meet the
needs of processing information with varying temporal
features.
Oxygen vacancies are a common type of point defect
that plays an essential role in regulating the physical and
chemical properties of metal oxides, such as electronic
distribution, ionic migration, and band structure of metal
oxides.24,25 For instance, since perovskite manganese
oxide semiconductor preferred an oxygen-rich state,
applying positive/negative voltage pulses to the gate can

control the generation/filling of oxygen vacancies in the

Moreover, as one of the intrinsic defects in metal oxides,
oxygen vacancies could act as deep donors, and dominate
the trapping phenomenon of nonequilibrium carriers. In
view of the potential associations between the oxygen
vacancies and hole trapping, the a-GaOx synaptic device
with the highest content of oxygen vacancies exhibits the
most pronounced paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) effect,
and induces nonlinear neuromorphic features of the
photo-synapse.27 Thus, utilizing the controllable modula-
tion ability of device conductance based on oxygen
vacancies, PRC has been implemented for tasks including
fingerprint recognition,27 voice recognition,13,24 and mul-
timodal recognition.10 However, physical devices designed
to meet the computational requirements of both the reser-
voir and the output layer through the modulation of oxy-
gen vacancies have not yet been reported.
In this article, by leveraging the tuning effect of oxy-
gen vacancies on the pentacene/ZnO energy barrier, an
STM reservoir device (ZnO-50% device) with a broad
range ratio of τ and LTM output device (ZnO-Ar device)
with strong charge trapping and retention properties
were implemented within the same device structure of
Cu/pentacene/ZnO/SiO2/Si. For ZnO-50% device, the τ
can be tuned over a larger range by varying the ampli-
tude and width of the electrical pulse. Furthermore, via
altering the gate bias, the ZnO-50% device exhibits a
broad range ratio of τ (>102). Inspired by the frequency
encoding of spatiotemporal information by ganglion cells
in the retina and the information reconstruction function
of the visual cortex, we proposed a homogeneous inte-
grated biomimetic obstacle recognition PRC to assist
visually impaired individuals in walking, which achieves
recognition accuracy up to 100% and 97.2% of obstacle
types and distances, respectively. This work offers an
effective strategy for realizing high-performance 3D-
integrated PRC chips in the future.

To elucidate the differences in charge trapping and
retention ability between the ZnO-50% and the ZnO-Ar
devices, we conduct the following analysis in conjunction
with the energy level structure of the materials. As shown
in Figure 4A, when a positive voltage pulse was applied
to the gate, the external electric field drove the electrons
injected from the electrodes to move downward. These
electrons were partially trapped by the defects at the
pentacene/ZnO interface, while another part was trapped
by the oxygen vacancies in ZnO after crossing the energy
barrier of the pentacene/ZnO. The trapped electrons will
induce more holes in the channel, leading to an increase
in IDS. After the pulse was removed, the negative gate
bias and the internal electric field generated by the
trapped electrons will drive the electrons to return to
the channel and recombine with the holes, resulting in
the decay of IDS. Compared with the ZnO-Ar thin film,

A low energy barrier facilitated more electrons being
trapped by oxygen vacancies during the pulse period
(Figure S11), leading to a larger ΔIDS. At the same time,
the low energy barrier also made it more difficult for the
trapped electrons to remain in the ZnO layer after
the pulse was removed (Figure 4B). As a result, ZnO-50%
device exhibited smaller memory window and stronger
STM. In contrast, the ZnO-Ar device, with a higher
energy barrier, exhibited a larger memory window and
enhanced LTM (Figure 4C,D).
Subsequently, to assess the capabilities of ZnO-50%
and ZnO-Ar devices to act as a reservoir physical node,
the range ratio of τ (τmax=τmin) and feedback strength of
the two devices under single-pulse stimulation with dif-
ferent conditions were extracted, respectively. In RC, the
computational capability of the system is closely related
to whether the physical nodes in the reservoir can effec-
tively capture different temporal characteristics and map
these characteristics to reservoir space.41,42 To expand the
number of effective reservoir node states, thereby provid-
ing as large a reservoir size as possible, the τ needs to be
tuned over as wide a range as possible. Because the broad
range ratio of τ allows the reservoir to flexibly tune τ
according to the timescale of the input signal, it enables
the effective extraction of separable input features when
processing complex information, thereby improving the
recognition accuracy (Note S1). The extraction method
for τ was described in Note S2. As shown in Figures 4F,

To test the ability of the ZnO-50% device to process
consecutive temporal information, the PPF effect was
simulated. As shown in Figure S19, although the condi-
tions of the two stimuli were identical, the ΔIDS of the
latter was significantly higher than that of the former,
indicating the facilitatory effect on synaptic plasticity.

Based on the above discussion, by leveraging the
modulating effect of oxygen vacancies on the energy level
structure of ZnO thin films, ZnO-50% device for the reser-
voir and ZnO-Ar device for the output layer have been
realized. Due to the same device structure of the reservoir
and output layer devices, the homogeneous integrated
all-PRC can simplify the complexity of the device
manufacturing process (Table S4). Additionally, the syn-
chronized manufacturing process of the reservoir and
output layer devices can also improve the stability of the
PRC performance. The MNIST handwritten digit data
was used as the object of recognition to verify the feasibil-

IDS of the LTM ZnO-Ar device, as shown in Figure S24).
Owning to the STM and rich separation characteristics
resulting from the electron trapping and de-trapping pro-
cesses in ZnO-50% device, the PRC exhibited excellent
image recognition accuracy (>90%, Figure 4J).

transformed into electrical activity by the cone/rod cells
in the retina and then sent to bipolar and horizontal
cells
for
further
processing
(Figure

reservoir should be able to separately respond to different

To explore the potential of the previously constructed
PRC in biomimetic obstacle recognition applications, the
response characteristics of the ZnO-50% device to contin-
uous pulses of different frequencies were first tested.
With the premise of a fixed pulse duration of 1 s, the IDS
of the ZnO-50% device exhibited a well-separated charac-
teristic that gradually decreased with the increase of
pulse frequency (Figure S25). This is because when the
total pulse stimulation time is the same, the number of
electrons trapped during a single pulse decreases as the
frequency
increases,
and
the
electrons
are
quickly
detrapped, ultimately leading to a reduction in the total
response current and a slower decay rate. Subsequently,
the mapping characteristics of the ZnO-50% device in
response to pulses of different sequences and frequencies
were tested. To effectively couple the temporal pulse
information in the input signal, the selection process
should ensure that the time interval of the input pulses is
less than the τ of the reservoir (Note S3). Therefore, the τ
(≈2.0 s) of the ZnO-50% device under 10 V, 500 ms pulse
stimulation was used as the duration for a single
sequence (Table S5). During the encoding process, the
input signal represented by “1” was divided into a series
of consecutive, shorter-duration pulse sequences at equal
intervals according to frequency (Figure S26). After the
pulse sequence, the response IDS is sampled and used as
the reservoir state (Figures S27 and S28). The non-
overlapping response of the 4-bit pulses at different fre-

map spatial information (Figures 5D and S29). Further-

frequency
sequences
are

distinguishable current states under the same sequence
stimulation from 2 to 32 Hz. Moreover, the reservoir
states under stimulation of different frequencies and
sequences were extracted (Figure 5F). Eighty pulse
sequences ranging from 2 to 32 Hz generated eighty
clearly distinguishable states, indicating that the ZnO-
50% device possesses a large reservoir size and the
capability
to
process

across

Based on the above discussion, a dataset composed of
various types and distances of obstacles that visually
impaired individuals may encounter in their daily lives
was constructed to verify the feasibility of biomimetic
obstacle recognition (Figure S31). The dataset consists of
600 binary images (60  60 pixels) of “Bicycle”, “Car”,
“Pedestrian”, “Telegraph pole”, and “Tree” at four differ-
ent distances. Since the timescale of input information
varies in different application scenarios, it is necessary to
match the τ of the reservoir according to specific circum-
stances (Table S6). In biomimetic obstacle recognition, to
associate distance, frequency, and the τ of the ZnO-50%
device, “Far”, “Medium”, “Near”, and “Close” corre-
spond to 4, 8, 16, and 32 Hz, respectively (Figure S32).
Consequently, the spatiotemporal information of external
objects was encoded into a series of 4-bit pulse sequences
of different frequencies (total time for each sequence was
2.0 s). These pulses were fed into the ZnO-50% device
and dynamically output the reservoir states (Note S4). As
shown in Figures 5G and S33, the recognition accuracy of
PRC for obstacle types gradually increased as the distance
decreased. At the closest distance, an accuracy rate of
100% can be achieved. In addition to identifying obstacle
types, the capability of PRC to recognize distances was
further tested. Since the τ of the ZnO-50% device can be
flexibly adjusted by the pulse width, the coupled IDS gen-
erated by different frequency stimuli can be separated
from each other. This characteristic endowed the PRC
with excellent recognition accuracy in the distance dis-
crimination of different obstacles (>91%, Figures 5H and
S34). Besides, the PRC showed a lower recognition accu-
racy after removing the reservoir (Figures S35 and S36),
which further demonstrated the importance of ZnO-50%
device in the effective processing of spatiotemporal infor-
mation. The above results confirm the feasibility of the
proposed oxygen vacancies modulation-based PRC in
handling biomimetic obstacle recognition with multi-
timescale. Additionally, Note S5 further discussed the
potential
of
the
tunability
of
τ
in
multi-scenario
applications.

CONCLUSION
By using the modulating effect of oxygen vacancies on
the energy level structure of ZnO, a homogeneous inte-
grated all-PRC with tunable temporal dynamics was
achieved. The ZnO-50% device, with a low concentration
of oxygen vacancies, exhibits STM characteristics with a

EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
4.1
|
Characterization
The surface structures of the ZnO thin films were investi-
gated using atomic force microscopy (AFM, Bruker's
Dimension Icon Atomic Force Microscopy) operated in
the tapping mode. The optical absorbance spectra of the
films were acquired using a UV–vis–near-infrared spec-
trometer (UV-3600, Shimadzu, Tokyo, Japan). UPS mea-
surements were performed by a Kratos Axis Supra with
He I (21.22 eV) as the excitation source.
4.2
|
Device fabrication and
measurement
The heavily doped n-type Si wafer with 90 nm SiO2 was
washed in acetone, ethanol, and deionized water with
ultrasonic for 10 min successively, treated in UV/ozone
for 10 min. The ZnO-50% and ZnO-Ar thin films were
prepared by RF sputtering under conditions of argon to
oxygen flow rate ratios of 12 sccm:12 sccm and 24 sccm:0
sccm, respectively. The preparation power was 100 W for
both. The semiconductor layer of 50 nm thick pentacene
was deposited onto ZnO layer by thermal vacuum evapo-
ration.
Finally,
100 nm
Cu
films
were
thermally
evaporated through a shadow mask to form source and
drain electrodes. The channel length (L) and width (W)
were 150 and 1500 μm, respectively. All the devices
were synchronously fabricated at the same conditions
and characterized in a shielding box under an ambient
air environment (RH = 20%) connected with a Keithley
2636B source meter.

Abstract: Physical reservoir computing (PRC) offers an effective computing paradigm for spatiotemporal information processing with low training costs. Achieving con- trollable regulation over the temporal dynamics of devices to meet the compu- tational demands of each physical layer is a key challenge for realizing high- performance PRC chips. Here, we proposed a homogeneously integrated all- PRC with tunable temporal dynamics. Utilizing the modulation effect of oxy- gen vacancies on the energy barrier of the pentacene/ZnO interface, short- term memory, and long-term memory switching characteristics have been achieved within the same device structure. Furthermore, by altering the gate voltage, the reservoir exhibited a broad range ratio of temporal characteristics (>102), which provides the potential to map information with different tempo- ral characteristics. Inspired by the process of encoding and reconstructing spa- tiotemporal information in the human visual system, a biomimetic obstacle recognition system has been constructed to assist visually impaired individuals in walking, demonstrating excellent accuracy in obstacle types (100%) and dis- tances (97.2%) recognition. This work offers a promising avenue for the devel- opment of an integrated PRC system with multi-timescale information processing capability.
